titleStmt.title: Formal Development of Real-time Priority-based Schedulers

analytic.title: Formal Development of Real-time Priority-based Schedulers

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: We introduce a deductive method for constructing realtime scheduling programs, based on continuous action systems and the higher-order logic of the refinement calculus. The schedulability goal is a guarantee that all the tasks meet their deadlines, at run-time. This analysis reduces to checking that "always" temporal properties hold on the task set, by enforcing adequate invariance properties. The initial, conjunctive model of the real-time system is further transformed, through refinement, into a program that obeys a specific scheduling policy. We exemplify our method on the Deadline-Monotonic and the Earliest-Deadline-First algorithms.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Nobody likes missing deadlines. However, in real-time systems, that is, systems whose correctness depends on both the accuracy of the output result, as well as on the time at which the latter has been delivered, late task completion can have much more severe consequences than at the individual level. When building a real-time schedule, it is essential to find a systematic way that guarantees that the tasks are executed while respecting the required timing constraints (deadlines). Such an algorithm is called a scheduling policy [9,12].

In practice, undesired effects like race conditions and deadlocks can be avoided by applying well-known resource control protocols. However, their programming discipline is not well supported by existing development tools. Thus, a rigorous, mathematically proven correct-by-construction methodology, for building generic real-time schedulers, is of great benefit.

We introduce, in this paper, such a precise method for the stepwise construction of real-time schedulers. Most of the previous formal approaches targeting real-time system verification or construction use symbolic, synthesis algorithms, intended for model-checking a closed real-time model [1,11]. The practical complexity of such algorithms is usually high. Our technique is purely deductive, and uses continuous action systems (CAS) [5] as the modeling language, and refinement calculus [7] as the correctnesspreserving reasoning environment. The CAS formalism is a state-based specification language for real-time and hybrid systems. It is supported by action-and system-level refinement rules, which lets us derive, in a correct manner, implementable models.

The method that we introduce leads, eventually, to an implementation of the real-time system model, still as an action system. This is achieved in a guided, correct manner, backed by the system refinement laws that we apply on the way. We exemplify the proposed construction strategy on the Deadline-Monotonic (DM) scheduling approach, which is a fixed-priority policy that provides exact schedulability tests for sporadic or periodic processes.

We consider tasks to be independent, and also abstract from their respective functionalities. We disregard any other resource allocation other than the CPU, too. For the DM scheme, we integrate scheduling theory results with incremental development within refinement calculus.

Employing a similar technique, we tackle the development of Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) scheduling programs. This is completed by a simulation-based validation method, where the constructed model is simulated up to the least-common-multiplier of the periods of the participating tasks. The simulation is carried out with the CAS symbolic simulator [4], built in Mathematica [16].

div.head: Enforcing the Required Conditions
div.p: A real-time scheduler can be seen as a task-set controller that has to be able to enforce certain properties, during the execution of the system. One of these properties, which assumes constraints on clocks, is called the schedulability condition, which requires that all task instances complete by their deadlines. Since this condition has to hold for any behavior of the system, it follows intuitively that it can be expressed as an "always" (2) temporal property. Given the definition of the "always" property over discrete behaviors [8], we can say that, for timed behaviors b (a sequence of states, where each state is a tuple of the form < (x, y) >, x and y being the local and the global variables), we have that: b |= 2 q iff (∀i

Assuming a discrete AS, Back and von Wright show how to prove enforcement of temporal properties by using invariant-based methods [8]. In order to effectively enforce the schedulability and other necessary predicates on sets of tasks, we propose a similar proof rule for the real-time case, as shown in Lemma 1. The rule states that proving the always property for the loop of the action system RTS, with the precondition of the loop established by the initialization (p ⊆ I), is in fact equivalent to showing that a predicate I ⊆ q is an invariant of RTS. It then follows that, if the conditions of Lemma 1 hold, the required constraints are enforced, thus a feasible schedule is constructed.
Targeting such a correct schedule, we start with a conjunctive representation of the loop of RTS, that is, we write do {Choice.I} ; Choice od, where
div.formula: Choice ∧ = g 1 .now → S 1 ; N [] . . . [] gn.now → Sn ; N
div.p: The information supplied by the computed precondition {Choice.I} is then used to refine the initial model, as shown in section 4.

Besides the invariant (denoted by I s , I s ⊆ q s ) that needs to hold in order to guarantee schedulability, two other types of constraints have to be enforced, for the real-time system to operate correctly. They are the mutual exclusion, and the scheduling policy conditions, that is, I me ⊆ q me , and I pol ⊆ q pol , respectively. The first one ensures that no more than one task at a time is granted the CPU, while the second imposes the order in which tasks are given priorities for execution. Thus, the predicate I in Lemma 1 is defined as
div.formula: I ∧ = I s ∩ I me ∩ I pol .
div.p: In general, the invariant I s involves constraints on clocks, which can not be checked statically. Therefore, one known approach for validating the schedulability of a task set is the simulation of the model, for a sufficiently long time, until the real-time system is in the periodic state. This interval of time is called the feasibility interval. We apply this method of validation by simulating the real-time CAS model that we construct, for the EDF protocol. To accomplish this task, we use the CAS symbolic simulation tool [4], built in Mathematica [16].

div.p: We restrict the model to tasks with D[i] ≤ P [i]. Tasks may be periodic, thus arriving at fixed intervals equal to the periods P [i], respectively, or sporadic, meaning that they have irregular arrival patterns, yet arriving at no less than P [i]. A fixed-priority scheduling policy relies on assigning priorities to tasks, offline. These priorities do not change during execution. One of the most popular such algorithm is the Deadline-Monotonic scheme, introduced by Leung and Whitehead [14].

div.head: Dynamic-Priority Algorithms : EDF
div.p: For dynamic priority schedulers, the priority of a task is recomputed at run-time. Within the context of uniprocessor scheduling, it has been shown by Liu and Layland [12] that the EDF algorithm, which at each instant of time chooses for execution the currently-active job with the smallest relative deadline, is an optimal algorithm. This means that any feasible task system is guaranteed to be successfully scheduled using EDF.
Non-preemptible Task Model. Given n periodic, nonpreemptible real-time tasks (with

div.formula: I edf pol ∧ = ∀i • ∀t ∈ [start, now) • state[i].start = ex ⇒ (∀j = i • (state[j].t = sl ∧ ca[j].t < P [j]) ∨ (state[j].t = wt ∧ D[j] -ca[j].t > D[i] -ca[i].t))
div.p: The condition I edf pol says that, once a task has moved to state ex, it either has been the only task waiting to be granted the CPU, or if other tasks have also been waiting simultaneously, the chosen task has the smallest relative deadline (the smallest difference between the absolute deadline D[i] and the arrival time) of them all.

div.p: Example. Suppose that we want to build an EDF schedule for the task set of Figure 1. 15), where T np (i) is replaced by T np (i) f . In order to validate this model, we use the simulation technique. We have to simulate (15), up to the least-commonmultiplier of task periods, which is t = 60, in our case.

For this purpose, we use the CAS simulator [4], built in Mathematica. The tool translates the guards and action bodies of the model in the language of Mathematica, and then uses a routine that goes through the guards, evaluates their boolean expression, one by one, and based on the resulted values, it computes the minimum moment of time as the next now; afterwards, the program detects the enabled actions, and selects one of them for execution. In case more actions are enabled at some time now, the user is supplied with the choice list of currently enabled actions, such that one of them is chosen for execution. There is also a programmed random mode, in which case the machine does the selection in a nondeterministic manner. The implemented model contains three guarded actions that abort the simulation in case any of the deadlines is missed. Simulation results. The essential information delivered by the above procedure is a list of time moments (now list) at which some action has been executed in the model, a corresponding list of actions (which we omit here), and lists with symbolic values for the discrete and continuous functions: the state of each task at each particular transition time, and the clocks ca1, ca2, ca3 as (continuous) linear functions of time. Figure 2 shows the mentioned symbolic lists.

In the Mathematica implementation, we have encoded the possible values, sl, wt, ex, of the state variables (state1, state2, state3) of each task, as 0, 1, 2. One can see, in Figure 2, based on these values, the order in which tasks have been executed, at each moment of time now, given in the corresponding now list. The tasks are deemed to share a critical instant, at time 0, as, initially, all of them are in state = 1, waiting for the CPU. So, naturally, the first to execute is task 3, since at time 0, it has the earliest deadline, after which task 2, and task 1 follow. Note that, at time now = 60, the simulation scenario repeats itself. At the end of the simulation period, we also get the functions of time, state1, state2, state3, ca1, ca2, ca3, represented as graphs. In Figure 3, we present the timing diagram of our constructed schedule. Because all the imposed timing constraints hold during the feasibility interval, assuming worst-case execution times of participating tasks, we can declare the task set of the example, schedulable.

div.head: Conclusions and Related Work
div.p: We have presented a novel method for the incremental construction of scheduled systems, within the correctnesspreserving framework of continuous action systems and refinement calculus. Our development method starts with a conjunctive specification of the real time system, and applies refinement rules of propagating context assertions, in order to enforce the required schedulability, mutual exclusion and scheduling policy conditions. The generic method is applied to the DM, and EDF scheduling algorithms.
By simulating the EDF model of a simple set of three tasks, we obtain symbolic lists of transition moments, and of variable values, facilitating the schedule visualization.

Formal approaches have been recently applied by Kwak et al. [11], and Altisen et al. [1], who provide symbolic bisimulation and synthesis algorithms, respectively, to construct real-time schedules. A major disadvantage of these approaches is the practical high complexity of the algorithms, thus the methods can not accommodate a large number of tasks. In contrast, our schedulers have a general form.

The closest work to ours is due to Altisen et. al. [2], where fixed point computation algorithms are combined with the incremental application of priority rules that restrict the behavior of the initial timed-automata model.

Alur and Henzinger have specified preemptive schedulers as hybrid automata [3]. Their methods use model checking algorithms for verifying safety and liveness properties, thus suffering from similar drawbacks as the previously mentioned works.
We do not claim that our method is a panacea, we just believe it might serve as a useful alternative to modelchecking algorithms.
